references.text: Peter and John fixed their gaze on the lame man—the same Greek word (ἀτενίζοντες) is used to describe intense attention directed at a person.
The disciples looked up toward heaven as Jesus was taken up—the same expression (ἀτενίζονtes) for fixing one's gaze intently on someone.
Everyone in the Sanhedrin fixed their gaze on Stephen and saw that his face was like an angel's face—a parallel situation where everyone in a gathering stares intently at one person.
Paul in the synagogue at Antioch of Pisidia—he stood up in the synagogue and spoke, a parallel to Jesus' synagogue appearance in Luke 4.
The context for this verse: Jesus stood up to read in the synagogue and was handed the book of the prophet Isaiah, which he opened and read from.
The following verse where Jesus begins to speak to them after sitting down, showing that sitting down was the introduction to the teaching.
Jesus sat down (ἐκάθισεν) to teach the disciples—in Jewish tradition, the teacher sat down as a sign that the teaching had begun.
The scribes and Pharisees sit on Moses' seat—sitting down is the authoritative teaching position in the synagogue and Jewish tradition.
Ezra opened the scroll before the people, and when he opened it, all the people stood up—a parallel to public Scripture reading in a gathering.
Jesus fixed his gaze on them (ἐμβλέψας)—a similar situation where Jesus' intense gaze is connected with an important announcement.
